entry.title: Lo viejo funciona, Juan! A monolithic is enough, almost ever.
entry.summary: It is a common saying: ‘You will need a MVP ready as fast as you can.’ I need a landing page with a contact form to input their email and user’s name. Great! npm create vite@latest I will develop a ReactJS project with router, so any case the user writes the URL wrong, I can redirect them to the homepage again. I will split the code into many components. One for the header, the other is the footer, a Main-content wrapping the different sections. Then, I also need an API in NodeJS to send the email. A POST route for the form, GET route for checking the API’s health. GET default route for index. I was thinking about using express-xss-sanitizer middleware for security reasons, and Jest for unit testing. But we are forgetting the KISS. Where is the love? KISS rule is Keep it simple s… Instead of all these files, routes, packages, and repositories. What if we develop a simple HTML with CSS. You can use Tailwind, and GSAP, loading with a CDN if it makes the development faster. But you truly don’t need React for a simple landing page. Is it the old way to do it? Yes, but it is easier and faster. You will have time to make your micro-service architecture any time later. The main goal of a developer is to fix any problem as fast as possible. If you can make it cheaper, better :D You can also do it with no-code apps like Wix, Webflow, Carrd, etc. I know that. However, this post is for developers, not for entrepreneurs. If you are not a developer, you should definitely go to no-code apps. They will make your life easier. However, what I am trying to debate here, is that we (developers) always think about the first rule: DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself), but we always forget about the second KISS rule. It is important to balance both. :D

entry.title: Performance Tuning: Linux Kernel Optimizations for 10k+ Connections
entry.summary:
1. Introduction
In high-concurrency real-time architectures, the performance bottleneck inevitably shifts from the application layer to the operating system. A well-optimized Flask-SocketIO application running on Gevent or Eventlet is theoretically capable of handling tens of thousands of concurrent connections. However, in a default Linux environment, such an application will likely crash or stop accepting connections long before CPU or memory resources are saturated. This plateau occurs because the Linux kernel, out of the box, is tuned for general-purpose computing, not for acting as a massive termination point for persistent TCP connections. Why I Ditched Terminal UIs for Recruiters
entry.summary:
Why I Ditched Terminal UIs for Recruiters
I built a terminal-style portfolio. Black screen. Commands. ASCII vibes. very me. And almost everyone said the same thing: “This is cool… but recruiters won’t get it.” They were right. Terminal portfolios are fun for developers. You’re technical You’re confident You like bending conventions But recruiters don’t explore. They skim. They want: Who are you? What do you build? Can I understand this in 10 seconds? A blinking cursor asking them to type help already lost half the room. My terminal UI wasn’t failing because it was bad. It was failing because it required participation. Recruiters don’t want to interact. recognize. That’s when it clicked: signal amplifier. I rebuilt my portfolio as: UI-first Motion-driven Immediately readable Big typography. Same personality. Different delivery. The irony? after I made it simpler. Cool ideas still need clear entry points A portfolio is not for you, it’s for your audience You can still be creative without being cryptic I didn’t kill the terminal UI idea. I rebuilt my portfolio to be UI-first, motion-heavy, and recruiter-readable If you want to see what that pivot looks like in practice: 👉 https://zeno-guy-portfolio.vercel.app/ Fair warning: I still overengineered it. Just more responsibly this time.

entry.title: My Very First Blog Post
entry.summary: I've always wanted to learn how to code, so in 2024 I got a job that allowed me to save up enough money to buy myself a PC (it was my friend's PC ). It was literally the best experience of my life, I went on YouTube watching every web development video I could get my hands on. From there I progressed to downloading tutorials from a particular source 🌚. I was enjoying the tutorials until I got to a point where I was struggling a bit to watch another lecture video. Eventually I finished a course on HTML and CSS, I thought that was it... I had learnt how to code, that narrative changed when I actually sat down to build an actual project on my own without the help of any tutorial, that was when I realized that I still have a long way to go. I decided to take up coding challenge from Frontend mentor (A site with Frontend projects) to reinforce my learning with HTML and CSS, and to be honest I saw the extent of my limit, it was frustrating and at the same time annoying. I then went back to the basics which helped me actually attempt a few challenges, I was happy to see I was making tiny improvements, right now I've built upto 8 frontend mentor projects, and I don't intend on stopping there. Well that's it for now. I'm gonna look back at this one day and go wow! I've made progress.
